speakeroldname: Mr. R. C. MATTHEWS (Toronto East Centre):
subtopic: REPORT OF FINDINGS OF COMMITTEE ON INQUIRY INTO PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to present the fourth report of the select standing committee on banking and commerce dealing with the price of gasoline. The report is as follows:
The select standing committee on banking and commerce begs leave to submit its fourth report as follows:
Your committee has had under consideration an order of reference, dated February 11, 1932,-
"That, in the opinion of this house, the price of gasoline to the Canadian consumer has for some time past been too high, and that this matter should be referred to the select standing committee on banking and commerce to investigate and report."
Your committee has held 22 meetings, and has taken viva voce evidence on oath of 20 witnesses. Numerous exhibits were filed by witnesses.
The aforementioned witnesses represented the following companies:
Imperial Oil, Limited,
McColl-Frontenac Oil Company, Limited,
British American Oil Company, Limited,
Shell Oil of Canada, Limited,
Eastcrest Oil Company, Limited,
2984	COMMONS
Banking and Commerce-Report
and also included individual importers and distributors, in some cases importing direct from the United States, and in other cases purchasing gasoline from Canadian refiners.
An officer of the White Star Refinery Company, of Detroit, Michigan, also gave evidence concerning the condition of the petroleum industry in the United States.
An official of the customs branch of the National Revenue department gave evidence respecting the appraisal of petroleum imports for duty purposes.
The Clarkson commission report of 1926 to the Ontario government, being a report of an inquiry into the prices of gasoline and oils sold in the province, is incorporated in the evidence taken by your committee.
A committee of the legislature of Saskatchewan was concurrently conducting a similar inquiry to that of your committee, but within the limitations of provincial jurisdiction, and presented a report of its findings and recommendations to the legislature.
The said Saskatchewan committee report is not within the order of reference from the house to your committee and therefore has not been considered by your committee but in view of the recommendations therein contained has been incorporated in the printed proceedings of evidence in order that the house may be informed of its contents.
Pursuant to authorization given by the house, your committee engaged the firm of George A. Touche & Company, chartered accountants. This firm was instructed as follows, namely:-
1.	That the accounts of the Imperial Oil, Limited, be taken for the purpose of establishing the fundamental facts required by the committee.
2.	That a basis of establishing the ascertainment of costs be mutually agreed upon between the auditors and the officers of Imperial Oil, Limited.
3.	That for the purposes of the two preceding paragraphs, the investigation be specifically applied against
(a)	The Sarnia and Halifax refineries as regards the elements entering into production costs as a 'whole and as applicable to proportionate distribution of these total costs against gasoline and other commodities refined from crude.
(b)	The relative wholesale prices of gasoline and other commodities refined from crude in relation to costs of production at the Sarnia and Halifax refineries.
(c)	The elements embodied in the selling, distribution and administration expenses, added to the costs of production, in relation to selling prices for Imperial Oil, Limited, as a whole and as specifically applied in the following marketing divisions-
(d)	That such marketing divisions may be designated by your sub-committee.
4.	That synonymous with this investigation by the auditors into the aforementioned cost and selling factors of the Imperial Oil, Limited, they secure from British American Oil Co., Limited, and from McColl-Prontenac Oil Co., Limited, statements in such form as will render practicable a comparison of the relative costs and selling prices of the three corporations, thus offering means of disclosing any major variations without entailing the additional expense of investigating the smaller oil companies operating in Canada.
IMr. Matthews.}
The auditors were also directed to make an examination and audit of the books of the MeCdll-Frontenae Oil Company with respect to certain operations of that company.
The auditors' report was duly presented to your committee by Mr. 0. A. Matthews, a member of the firm of George A. Touche and Company, who explained in detail the clauses of the report as the same was read at presentation. Mr. Matthews was subsequently recalled, sworn and examined in respect to matters connected with the audit and report. Statements of figures abstracted from the books of the audited companies, and extended in the report, were duly filed.
A summary of the conclusions as set out in the auditors' report is as follows:
(a)	That the company's records relating to 1930 operating costs charged to gasoline showed no evidence of "cost loading" by reason of affiliations in the United States and South America, or because of unfavourable accounting practices, but rather, that the gasoline costs, if anything, were understated because of the company's conservative policies in not loading into costs such matters as fire insurance premiums, depreciation rates, contingency reserve charges and inventory pricing.
(b)	That the total costs for 1930 were free of charges for interest on capital invested, or such as might be related against funded debt or as a charge imposed by a parent company in the form of rental for use and operation of the refineries and marketing stations and equipment. In other words, the financing of Imperial Oil, Limited, has been effected through the sale of capital stock and the investment of a proportion of surplus earnings in extensions of plant and equipment facilities, without any issue of bonds or debentures upon which interest might be charged.
(c)	That the 1930 marketing costs charged to gasoline whilst as a whole legitimate from an accounting point of view, were high in relation to total costs. The high cost of marketing is attributed to territorial and climatic conditions, and extreme competition obtaining in the distribution and marketing of gasoline in Canada. In view of the fact that the territorial and climatic conditions in Canada are not subject to human manipulation and change, a partial solution of the problem would seem to lie in a concerted action on the part of all distributing companies to eliminate as far as possible the present costly system of marketing.
(d)	That variations in gasoline prices in 1929, 1930 and 1931 to consumers were not based directly upon ascertained refinery costs, but largely upon the variations in the market cost of crude oil with fluctuating additional charges for excise tax, sales tax, freight surcharge and exchange. It has not been demonstrated that any grounds exist for any allegations that the company has taken unfair advantage of either the specific or dumping duties in its gasoline prices to consumers during the period under investigation.
(e)	That the reason for the unfavourable comparison at some points between United States competitive prices and those of the Imperial Oil, Limited, is due to the demoralized condition of the gasoline industry in the United States, caused by the over-production of gasoline and various tax evasion "rackets," which, in turn, result in the price of United

Banking and Commerce-Report
States gasoline falling far below the relative movements in crude oil prices and other costs of production and distribution.
(f)	That the zoning basis of establishing gasoline prices results in the spreading of transportation differentials' to the comparative disadvantage of gasoline consumers at centres of trade in proximity to some refineries, whereas the zoning price basis frequently operated to the advantage of gasoline consumers in the territories outlying from the refineries. It was also found that tank wagon gasoline prices are given to farmers and coastal fishermen both east and west.
(g)	That in such outlying districts as have no dealer competition or where any dealer association arrangements exist, the spread between Imperial Oil, Limited, tank wagon prices and the prices to the consumer is entirely in the hands of the independent dealers.
(h)	That apart altogether from the basis used in the establishing of gasoline prices, the spread between such selling prices and the combined costs of refining and marketing showed an average net profit of not exceeding 1-01 cents per imperial gallon of all gasoline sold by Imperial Oil, Limited, in the year 1930.
(i)	That in view of the fact that the investigation of Imperial Oil, Limited, disclosed no improper accounting practices in the matter of costs or unstated profits, and because Imperial Oil, Limited, occupy the leading position in the gasoline industry in Canada, the auditors gave it as their opinion that the expense which would be involved in extending their investigation into the records of the British American Oil Company, Limited, the McColl-Frontenac Oil Company, Limited, and other oil companies in Canada, would not be justified in view of their findings on the average net profit per gallon of gasoline sold by Imperial Oil. Limited, in 1930.
From a consideration of the evidence and the auditors' report, it is the opinion of your committee that the price of gasoline to the Canadian consumer is not unreasonably high, and that the public interest would not be further served by a continuation of this inquiry.
Tabled herewith is a copy of the printed proceedings and evidence.
All of which is respectfully submitted.

subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBERS OF MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, that I was not here yesterday, owing to an engagement in my own city, and therefore could not register my opposition to the principle of this measure. I am grateful to the Prime Minister for giving me the opportunity of doing so to-day.
This measure is one of taxation, and according to my views it violates two great principles of British constitutional law with regard to taxation. First, the principle of equality. It is a well-known principle that in matters of taxation there should not be any discrimination. Everybody must be treated in the same way. In this bill there is a discrimination against a class. The judges of Canada, apart from being required to pay the income taxes every citizen of Canada has to do, are singled out for the purpose of levying upon their salaries a special additional tax of ten per cent. This is class legislation; there is no doubt about it. There is no more reason for it and no more justification for an additional income tax on judges than there would be for one on butchers or bakers or on people who happen to have red hair-

subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBERS OF MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext: Or who are baldheaded.

subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBERS OF MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext:
Or who are baldheaded, as my hon. friend from Southeast Grey says, or anybody else in a special category or class.
41761-188)
There is no doubt whatever that this measure is certainly opposed to one of the fundamental principles of taxation, that of equality of taxation, and it becomes an arbitrary levy upon a certain class of men. More than that, even in that class there is a discrimination because the bill applies only to the judges who are paid by the Dominion of Canada. The recorders, the provincial judges, the judges of police courts, although some of them have salaries almost as high as the salaries of the members of the high courts, are not taxed. I am sure that everybody upon second thought will agree with me that this is an absolutely vicious principle. Our income tax statutes are based on the theory that the taxes are levied in a certain proportion on the annual gain or annual means of every citizen of Canada. This is a deviation from that principle. Furthermore, Lord Phillimore, in the case of Caron versus the King, which was based on our federal income tax laws, recognized that principle. He said:
They-
Meaning the income tax acts of this dominion:
-are statutes for imposing on all citizens contributions according to their annual means, regardless of, or it may be said, not having regard to, the source from which their annual means are derived.
The tax is levied on the annual gain or means of every citizen; the law does not say where it comes from, and it is not fair, it is against the principle of the legislation that a certain class or a certain profession in the community should have imposed upon it special taxation different from that imposed on any other class. That is one principle that is violated by this bill. But there is another one.

subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBERS OF MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES

Quite right, but the judges are not exempted. They are paying the same tax in proportion . as any other citizen of Canada. This is the change. There was no change before this bill.
The other principle which is violated is the great British principle of no taxation without representation. The judges are not represented in this house. They have no vote here; they have no-

subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBERS OF MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext:
We were informed by the Prime Minister that most judges were willing to pay the ten per cent.
Mr, LAPOINTE: I have no concern about that; it is possible they are willing to pay. If so, let them pay voluntarily. My point is that this parliament has no right to impose a special tax on the judges of Canada through the operation of a special bill such as the one now before us. Nobody speaks for them. We have taken away from them not only the right to vote but the right to speak. They cannot defend themselves. They have no right to say anything on public matters, and may I say that the present legislation is not very generous or courageous; it is not sportsmanlike to attack people who have not the right to defend themselves. They can say nothing in their defence. More than that, we have passed legislation prohibiting them entering other gainful occupations. We have prohibited them from deriving any other income or revenue from any sources whatever, as do other people in times of prosperity. Now we are asking them-we are forcing them, in a period of depression, despite the fact that when times were better they had no opportunity to benefit-to pay a special tax.
There is no doubt that the legislation now before us is makeshift, because the government found it could not place them under the bill to reduce salaries. They are doing indirectly what they could not do directly. Judges are not servants of the crown. Since the Act of Settlement that fact has been well established and accepted. They sit in judgment on differences and difficulties arising between the crown and the subjects. They cannot be removed by the crown as can other
[Mr. Lapointe.1
civil servants. After the Act of Settlement another law was passed affecting only the judges and enacting that they are not related, as are other civil servants, to the sovereign; they are not servants of the crown. I quite realize that the government could not have included them in the bill which has now become law. The present legislation, however, is only a subterfuge, and is opposed to the principles of British law. I know the Minister of Justice does not like it; he could not like it. I can remember very well a time when he blamed me for not taking the means to increase judges salaries. I can remember his eloquent words to the effect that judges are not paid adequately, and that in fact they were underpaid. Well, he is doing worse than I did; at least I did not reduce their salaries.
I know that in certain quarters it is stylish to attack judges. As I have already said they cannot defend themselves. The statement has been made that it is easy to find people prepared to accept a position on the bench. That may be so, but the present Minister of Justice knows as well as I do that it is difficult to find the men we would like to appoint to the higher courts of the land. Certainly it is possible to find some men, but let me tell hon. members that there is no doubt a poor servant is always overpaid. Let us suppose that we should apply the same principle to the House of Commons. When I came to parliament the indemnity was only $1,000. It was increased to $1,500, then to $2,500, and now it is $4,000. May I suggest that if it were again $1,000 quite possibly there would be people who would be willing to accept office. That, however, is not a fair basis upon which to decide the amount which should be paid to judges, to members of parliament or to any other servants of the people. I do not desire to say more in this connection except that it is of supreme importance to Canada that we should have an impartial and independent judiciary. I do not think it is right to subject judges to the necessity of looking to parliament to learn whether their salaries or taxes are going to be increased or decreased from year to year. Judges must be altogether independent of parliament; they must be fearless. They have a tremendous responsibility. We exact from them high standards of living, and as I said we exclude them from all other gainful occupations. We are proud of our Canadian bench, and I think we should make it so that our judiciary would be in a position to maintain the prestige with which it has always been surrounded.

Income War Tax Act
Last night when I entered the chamber the estimates of the Minister of National Defence were under review. There was discussion on an item of almost $2,000,000 for the training of the non-permanent militia. Let me tell hon. members that the country might more easily dispense with the training of the nonpermanent militia than impose a special tax on our judges. To please the hon. member for Southeast Grey may I say I would also be quite willing to cut off the amount set aside for cadet training, rather than make a levy on the salaries of judges.
There is another point upon which I should like to say a few words. The government was blamed for not having put a tax, similar to the one now under discussion, on the salaries of lieutenant-governors. Well, this one is bad, but the other one would also be bad. I have heard the suggestion in this house that we could very well dispense with the office of lieutenant-governor in the provinces. Well, my reply to that is that under the British North America Act the lieutenant-governor is part of the constitution; it is part of the legislature of a province. The act says that the legislature of the province of Quebec shall be composed of a lieutenant-governor, a legislative assembly and a legislative council. It states further that the legislature of Ontario shall be composed of a lieutenant-governor and a legislative assembly. Lieutenant-governors form part of legislative bodies. So long as we have autonomous provinces the lieutenant-governors represent the king in those provinces, and no hon. members in this parliament have the right to do away with that office in the provinces.
I am not sure either that the people of the provinces favour this change, and I know in Quebec they would not. In Quebec the office of lieutenant-governor is part of our national life. The home of the lieutenant-governor is the national home of the province. The lieutenant-governor represents the king; he represents law; he represents order; he represents authority. I do not think there would be even a very small minority in the province which would favour doing away with the lieutenant-governorship. Let me say also that the salaries of the lieutenant-governors are perhaps the only ones that have never been increased since confederation. All the other salaries have been increased; the lieutenant-governors are being paid to-day what they were paid in 1867. Is it to be suggested that we should have only wealthy people as representing the crown in the provinces? I am opposed to that suggestion. We have in my own province at the present time a lieutenant-governor whom I would not change for any
millionaire, no matter whence he came in this country; far from it; and he has the esteem, the good will and the affection of every citizen of the province. The salary which is being paid to the representatives of the crown, instead of being too large, in my opinion is much too small.
Those are the considerations I wanted to express to-day, and I am thankful to the Prime Minister for having given me the opportunity of doing so,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBERS OF MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with a
great deal of the speech of my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) I am in hearty accord, but with some of the opinions which he has offered to the house I cannot agree. We all realize that it is not a pleasant nor an agreeable thing either on the one hand to impose taxation or on the other to reduce salaries. Measures of this kind are not brought forward unless there is some urgent necessity for them, and it was felt that at the present time there was an urgent necessity in Canada of decreasing expenditures in every direction. It is for that reason that the reduction of salaries in the civil service and extra taxation in regard to the judiciary are proposed. And the proposal is only for a single year.
My hon. friend has based his objections-upon two grounds. First, that it is illegal or unconstitutional to impose taxation upon the judges; secondly, that we are violating * principle in this measure by imposing taxation without representation. Viewed in regard to our strict legal rights, I think the matter is one upon which there cannot be very much division of opinion. We have in this parliament under the British North America Act authority to tax anything we see fit to tax. The powers of this parliament are practically unlimited in that respect; they are to be found in section 91. We are empowered to raise money by any mode or system of taxation. My hon. friend says that in this measure we do not propose a fair or general tax, but that we discriminate. In my humble opinion, we are entitled, if we see fit, to discriminate. That is our legal right.

speechtext: I did not say otherwise.

In this case we propose
not to discriminate, but to impose taxation upon all the members of a class, and that class consists of those who receive money by way of salary from the treasury of the dominion. My hon. friend points out that in his good

Income War Tax Act
province of Quebec there are a number of individuals who are not, strictly speaking, judges, but who are appointed by the province to administer law as in other provinces magistrates do. They are provincial officers, and we have not sought in any way to interfere with the salaries or emoluments which they receive. But all members of the judiciary who receive money from the federal treasury are under this proposal taxed in respect only of the salary which they receive from that treasury. That is the special tax that is imposed.
Now, on the legality of the proposal I submit there cannot be two opinions. As to the propriety of our doing so there may be a very great difference of opinion. Personally, I do not favour a reduction in judges' salaries, and under other circumstances I would not feel justified in imposing this taxation upon them. I remember the incident which my hon. friend referred to when I did urge in this house an increase in judges' salaries. It was at a time when there was affluence in the country, when our treasury was overflowing-

That is the operating
thought in my mind at all events; because in the main I agree with the position which my hon. friend has taken with regard to the judiciary of this country.
On the other branch of his case he submits we are not justified in taking this step because we should not impose taxation where there is no representation. Well, I submit that the judiciary of this country are represented in the House of Commons, not by themselves but by the representatives of the people of the country. If my hon. friend's argument is

correct, we could not impose taxation upon the civil servants, because the civil servants are not represented here except through the members of this house. Many bodies are not represented here; none of the officers of the government practically have a right to sit here or to be heard here. Now, I submit there is no foundation in fact for that objection; that this House of Commons represents the whole dominion, all classes of citizens of this country.
For these reasons I submit we are strictly on legal ground in bringing down this bill. I hope it will be only for a single year. The measure itself is so expressed; it will expire after the present year.
There is not unanimity among the judiciary themselves with regard to the measure. I have received letters supporting the proposal from a number of judges who desire to have this tax imposed upon them, or to make their contribution as others do; on the other hand, I have received communications from other judges objecting to the proposal. As I say, there is no unanimity among the judiciary in that respect. But judging the matter as a whole, reviewing the circumstances as we know them in this house since the bill was introduced, and particularly having regard to the desire on the part of everyone in Canada to reduce expenditure to the minimum, I believe the present bill is justified at this juncture and ought to be adopted.

I think there is a very sound objection on constitutional grounds. I agree with my hon. friend who just spoke that the judges are in a class by themselves. They are not civil servants; they are not the servants of the crown, and the time may come when they will be the buffer between the crown and the people. I do not believe there should be any interference with a contract made with a man when he ascends the bench. We surround him with limitations. He cannot engage in trade; as my hon. friend pointed out, he cannot accept any public office and he cannot sit in the parliament of this country. To a very large extent he is removed from the ordinary people of his locality. He cannot practise the profession for which he has been trained, and to my mind it would be an unfair thing, after he has accepted office and continued therein for a number of years, by force of an act of parliament to say that although we made a bargain with him, now his salary is to be reduced without his consent. To my mind that would be an unconstitutional act.

We know that an effort was made last autumn to reduce the salaries of judges in Great Britain, and we know that when the matter was discussed and fully inquired into the better opinion, both of lawyers and laymen, was that it would not be proper to reduce the salaries of the judges. Many very able legal opinions were expressed to the effect that it would be unconstitutional to do so. That is my own view, and that is why I would not feel free to support a statutory reduction in the salaries of members of the judiciary.

But the minister argued on the propriety of the matter, saying that we had no moral right to reduce the salaries of
judges because of their peculiar position. Now he goes ahead and moves that we tax them an additional ten per cent. I confess that, having a mind not capable of drawing fine philosophical distinctions, I cannot see the difference. If I may state the point of view which I hold in this matter, I believe that the salaries of judges should have been subject to the reduction imposed on every other member of the service. I am sorry to disagree in this matter with my colleague from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). I do believe that this legislation is perhaps the most vicious that has ever been introduced into this house, in that it discriminates between different classes of citizens and proposes to penalize certain people because they belong to a certain class. In other legislatures they take that action in connection with people who have become nuisances, such as hucksters, peddlers and people of that sort. We impose a special tax on them. We are now degrading those who should be the leaders in our social structure, the judges, members of the militia, members of the police force and others, to the level of common nuisances, and I protest against that action being taken.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to state that I entirely agree with the views expressed a short while ago by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). Judges have been placed in a special class, they have been deprived of numerous privileges that the humblest citizen of this country enjoys. To-day the

I wonder whether he is levying this special tax on the judges to enable him to meet the $2,000 increase which he granted to himself and his colleagues last year. To think that, in a crisis, when the revenues of Canada are not adequate to meeting the expenditures for administration, members of the government thought fit to vote themselves a salary increase of $2,000, and that, to-day, they state in the house that further revenue is required and a special tax of 10 per cent must be levied on judges to meet expenditure. me, there were quite a number of them. The hon. member was absent, but others were here.
As to the tax levied on judges, let us be fair. One may calmly comment on judges' salaries, however, for the same reason which the hon. member for Beauharnois has just pointed out, under present circumstances, I contend that it is neither fair to the judges, nor to the army and navy officers, nor to any class whatsoever of the community, to

Income War Tax Act
state that, in the present crisis, they should be exempt from shouldering their share of the public burden. If we wish to guard against the feelings of public hatred and distrust spreading against the leading classes, it behooves us not to advertise in our legislation and budget that we exempted certain classes on account of the position they occupy.
One hears: Judges are deprived of the right to exercise their franchise. Is it to penalize them that they are so deprived? Quite the contrary, it is to more clearly bring out the importance of the duties they discharge and shield them from the criticism of public opinion, it is to place them, so to speak, on a higher plane than the masses. It is not a punishment but an acknowledgment of the importance of their duties and the impartiality they are expected to show towards everybody.
Judges, at times, are called upon to decide on political cases. Take for instance the Controverted Elections Act, by which parliament desists from its inherent and constitutional right to decide upon legislative functions. It has transferred to the courts the exclusive right of passing judgment on all controverted election matters or the obtaining of a parliamentary mandate by corrupt or other underhand means. Why was this done? So as to make it clear that the intention was to defer to an absolutely unbiased mind, the duty of carrying out a legislative mandate.
And in order to enable judges to discharge impartially this all important duty, which, to some extent, is linked with the parliamentary mandate, they were removed from the seat of political strife. That is why they do not exercise their right to the franchise. I think it would be a mistake to look upon this loss, by which judges are disfranchised, as belittling their office. Quite the contrary it is an acknowledgment-how shall I express it-it is a recognition of the importance of their office, it is a mark of respect extended to them. However, to conclude from this that, in a country-Whether one likes it or not-in a democratic country a particular class of public servants-I use the word in its broadest sense-a particular class of public servants- whether they be lieutenant-governoi's, who are after all officials appointed by the Dominion government, or judges designated to their post by the Dominion government to carry out duties which are assigned to them by pai'liament, or again whether they are army or navy officers, who are so delegated by parliament to maintain peace or defend their country, why, I wonder, under the present circumstances, should we exempt them
from contributing their quota to the public exchequer? Again do I say that the hon. member for Beauharnois was perfectly justified in stating that it was highly improper on the part of the ministers of the crown to grant themselves a salary increase, and it was a very improper thing for parliament to unanimously endorse this increase. But the fact of having blundered last year in this connection, is not a reason to blunder to-day and proclaim to the country, when thousands of needy people are unable to find food for their everyday subsistence, that a certain class of people who happen to be wearing a three-cornered hat, or sit on the bench will be exempted or that another class of people who parade the streets with decorations on their breast, or again others who are travelling on ships either on the Atlantic or the Pacific, paid by the government to idle away the time, must be exempted from carrying their share of the burden. No, the time has come when all classes must shoulder their share of the burden.
As to the aim of this measure, I entirely approve what the government has stated or rather what it is doing to-day. It is possible that they are doing so to cover their retreat, that they are presenting it under the guise of income tax, instead of doing what would have been the right thing, namely: reduce the salaries of judges and officers like those of other civil servants. However, there is an old English proverb which applies to all public administrations: "Let them down easy." The moment they perform a worthy act I have no fault to find whether they slip out by the side door instead of coming through the front door. The fact that the result attained is the same, that all classes of the community contribute to the public fund, to the liabilities of the state, gives us sufficient ground to approve them and, for my part, I do it heartily.

The enumeration would be endless; so many things could be said. This measure is absurd and of a nature to bring discredit on the government. I am sufficiently well acquainted with the right hon. Prime Minister and his colleagues to know that they have no intention-to use a popular term-to fatten up at the government's expense. I do not deny that there may have been some abuse in connection with automobiles. I am not discussing this point at present; however, in a crisis the ministers who are responsible for the legislation in this house should first practise on themselves what an illustrious Japanese admiral, Admiral Nogi called "Hari-Kari". Should not the members of the government follow this example?
If the cut in the indemnity is necessary, I think the ministers should be the first to set the example.
It is not that the indemnity they receive for the duties they discharge is out of proportion; however, in a crisis ministers should not simply be satisfied with sacrificing the members and the civil servants of this country.
The right hon. Prime Minister, on his return from England, last year, made a statement, which was published by the Canadian press, and in which he appealed to private charity. Private charity responded most readily. People put into practice this admirable saying of Christ: "Love your neighbour as yourself and love one another." People helped one another. Numerous charitahle societies did marvellous deeds and private individuals made sacrifices to help their fellow citizens who were in poverty How was this charity carried out? By practising the most rigid economy. The 10 per cent taken, to-day, from the civil servants went to charity. One may think that 10 per cent is not much yet, throughout all the cities of Canada, in all the parishes and most remote villages, people set aside the poor man's share, expended a certain sum of money, part of their salary or income to feed those who were hungry, to quench the thirst of those who were thirsty and shelter those who had no home.
To-day with a cut of 10 per cent in their salaries, will private charity be able to do as much, in cooperation with the government,

as it did previously? Future will tell; however, we are inclined to believe that this salary reduction is untimely, that it has set a poor example to the country's capitalists whose eyes are always riveted on the tower of parliament, at Ottawa, and who eagerly read the newspapers so as to take their cue from higher up, from here, on Parliament Hill. I shall n-ot add anything further in this respect; however, previous to closing my remarks, I wish to make a humble suggestion to the government, as regards economy. By accepting, sir, the suggestion which I am going to make there wall be no further need of reducing the salaries of lieutenant-governors or judges. That is where my remarks refer to the question under discussion.
The hon. Solicitor General, since August 1930, has been the minister of the defeated candidates in Quebec. His part has been absolutely useless in the house. Last year, he was silent, and, this year, the government dispensed with his services, and according to the press, his leader did not forbid him to talk through his hat, but warned him not to talk through his large beaver hat. He played a useless part in Canada and also in Europe. That is why I request that the office of Solicitor General be done away with. His predecessor, the Hon. Lucien Cannon, pleaded a number of important cases before the Supreme Court, the Exchequer Court and the Privy Council. The present Solicitor General has not been called upon to plead any. He costs the country $40,000 per year. He has numerous secretaries. There is one to listen to what people are saying, another to interview those who come to his office, and another to reply to them. He is surrounded with a body guard, and reminds me of the former Czar Ferdinand of Bulgaria who never travelled without an armed guard. I do not wish to comment on the intellectual gifts of the Solicitor General, however, I think that the government would gain by dispensing with his services or, if the government are desirous of keeping him in their midst or circle, I would suggest that he be appointed Minister of Fisheries. That would be quite appropriate, because at least in Quebec, the fisheries would not fall under his control and he could therefore do no harm.
To sum up, sir, my suggestion is this: I think that, under the circumstances, the position of Solicitor General could be advantageously abolished, and the income could be distributed among charitable societies, such as the Red Cross, the Salvation Army, the St. Vincent de Paul and all the charitable societies which are doing so much good in this country. I have no personal ill-feeling against the Solicitor General. Personally, he seems to be a charming man, but here in the house we are obliged to consider things on their merits, and as, in my opinion, he has not done anything praiseworthy or wrong since he occupies his high office, I think the country would be better off if his services were dispensed with, within the shortest delay possible.

I am sure, with other
members of the committee, I am under a great obligation to the hon. member for Temiscouata for his voluminous exposition of the principles and the law that govern in a case of this kind. The classic defence of the position of a judge in this house was made by the late Judge Doherty. He was appointed to the bench when he was a young man of thirty-five or thereabouts. He served his fifteen years and was entitled to two-thirds of his salary as a pension which gave him $3,333.33 per annum. He was subsequently elected to parliament and later he became a minister of the crown. He was attacked in the old House of Commons for having received his pension while he was in receipt of pay as a member of parliament and as a minister of the crown. If hon. gentlemen are interested, they will find his defence recorded upon the pages of Hansard of that time. Shortly put-and I do not think it can be improved upon-it was this:	that having
entered into a contract with the crown to assume the obligations of judge, one of the terms of the contract being that after a certain number of years had elapsed he should receive a pension, he was entitled to that, having discharged his duties to the satisfaction of those to whom he was responsible and that no question could thereafter be raised because he was receiving the compensation provided for by the contract. The position with regard to judges is just that. They are not the servants of the crown; they are not the servants of the government. Under the Act of Settlement they occupy a very peculiar position. They are the administrators of the law; they constitute that branch of our government which we speak of as the judicial branch; they interpret our statutes and they administer the laws.
When my colleague the Minister of Justice said that it was not regarded as sound to decrease the compensation which judges receive by way of salary, he but stated a truism which might be indicated in another way. The contract is that they shall receive not less than (blank) dollars. However much more they may receive is for parliament to determine, but the contract of service is that they shall not receive less. In but two instances, I think, in all the history of the judicial branch of government in Great Britain has there been a reduction in salary and we recall in the early days the Master of the Rolls occupied a somewhat peculiar position. For many years he occupied a seat in the House of Commons and he was also Master of the Rolls. The Lord Chancellor to-day, of course occupying the highest posi-

tion in the judicial branch, of government in Great Britain, is also a political officer, being a member of the cabinet. The considerations that prevail here and in other overseas dominions with respect to the payment of salaries have no application in Great Britain, but the contract of every judge of every superior court in this country is that he shall receive not less than the stipulated sum provided for at the time he assumes office. In other words, if he gives up his practice at the bar and becomes a judge, there are two considerations that he must weigh before he takes the step. One is the salary, which will not be less than the sum provided by statute, and secondly, he has a retiring allowance which will not be less than the sum provided by statute. That completes the contract, and the reason the steps suggested were not taken when this measure with respect to the public service generally was submitted to this house was just what I have indicated. In Great Britain where, under the statute to which I made reference on that occasion, action was taken reducing the salaries of the judges by ten per cent, it was at once realized that a mistake had been made and in a very learned article that appeared in the Law Quarterly Review the reasons why that action should not have been taken were very clearly stated. Notwithstanding the observations made by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) it will be found at page 562 of Hansard for February 26 of this year that I made this observation:
The judges are not included in this measure. It has been contended by legal authority, and an article in the last issue of the Law Quarterly Review goes into the matter rather fully, that it would be a breach of the statutory rights of judges to undertake to make a curtailment in their salaries in this way. There are, however, other methods by which the matter may be dealt with, and the government has not finally determined what action it may take in that regard.
In other words, as long ago as the twenty-sixth of February when the resolution upon which the bill is founded was being introduced into this house, I had indicated that there were other methods by which the end might be accomplished. We were not prepared to break a contract. We were not prepared to determine by act of this parliament that the conditions under which the judges had undertaken to serve the state in their capacity as judicial officers should be set at naught, but I indicated that there were other methods by which, if thought desirable, the judges could be placed on an equality with other public servants, using the words public servants in the largest sense, in equality of

sacrifice. Immediately after the resolution was introduced and while it was still pending in this house, some of the judges wrote to my colleague, the Minister of Justice, others wrote to myself, and others to other members of the administration, saying that they desired at this time of stress and strain to make a contribution to the revenues of this country equivalent to ten per cent of their salaries. I may say for the information of this committee, Mr. Chairman, that the first letter I received was from a county court judge who had appeared before a special committee appointed by this house and given evidence as to the inadequacy of existing judicial salaries, pointing out that he could not with his family live on the salary he was receiving. Yet the first letter that I received from any judge suggesting that he would like to make a contribution of ten per cent of his salary to the state at this time came from that same judge. I thought that was a manifestation of a rather fine spirit. A chief justice was next, and there were other judges in all parts of the country. I will not say that the majority of them, because that would not be fair, and it would also be untrue, but several judges indicated their desire to make a contribution at this time of ten per cent of their salaries for the year. After it became apparent that numbers of them desired to make a contribution in that sense, the government in view of the expressions of opinion from all parts, of this house-for instance, if the exMinister of Justice and those associated with him had seen fit to make as strong observations with respect to interference in any way with judges' salaries as we have heard this afternoon, it is not probable that so strong an inference might have been drawn-

I accept at once my hon. friend's statement that he was not in the house when the matter came up, but certainly there were no expressions of opinion such as we have listened to to-day as to the undesirability of judges making a contribution this year to the public revenues. That is all that might fairly be said about the matter.
I would like to say that I. am one of those who in this house and outside of it, and I speak with some measure of diffidence because of. the positions I have occupied in my profession-it is somewhat difficult to speak as one really feels because it looks like special

pleading-have often said that the judges of this country are not adequately paid. The result has been a judicial body which does not as a whole reflect the genius of the legal profession in this country. I say that with very great frankness. I say that we should be able to improve the standard of judicial excellence in Canada. We have large numbers of judges by reason of the fact that we have a dual system. We, the federal power, appoint, and the provincial power determines the numbers. The result is that in almost every province of Canada there are more judges than there should, be, and instead of a few highly trained minds upon the bench you have large numbers of indifferent minds upon the bench administering justice. In the very nature of things that would be so;
The other day we had a striking illustration of the attitude of the British mind towards a position on the bench. One of the most eminent judges of our time, one who is a hereditary peer and occupied a great judicial position,. a man who came to this country some years ago, had said years ago that if the time ever came when any criticism was urged as to his age he would retire. When a resolution came before the House of Commons in England to increase the number of judges because it was found that for the moment judicial business was somewhat congested, the resolution passed after a speech had been delivered by the Solicitor General which invoked from one of the members a eulogy upon the subject w'hich he said had induced him to change his mind. He went on and made certain criticisms with respect to the age of this learned law lord, and the result was that within a few days, as you may have seen in the press, that distinguished jurist retired from his position. That is the effect of public opinion at once reflected upon the mind of a high-minded man who occupied as great a place in the judiciary as has fallen to the lot of any man to occupy in recent years. He retired at once under those circumstances.
In Canada there . has grown up in recent years a tendency to criticize the .judiciary unfairly. I attribute that to two things. First, the inadequacy of the salary makes it impossible to attract to the bench the best legal minds vre have. Secondly, and I am saying this in no over-critical sense or as indicating one party more than another, there has been too much political patronage concerned in appointments to the bench. The result has been that the test whether a man is entitled to a seat on the bench has seemed to be whether he has run an election and lost it. Very often that has been so. If he has run
an election and won it, peradventure he should not look for a seat on the bench because he can better serve his country in some other capacity. I know of cases in which eminent members of the bar have indicated that men who were wholly unfitted for judicial positions, as appeared within a very short time after their appointment, have been appointed to the bench. That happened because of a variety of circumstances and very often from the sense of obligation that men feel to those who have served their party with great faithfulness. In England on one occasion in the last fifty years there was a slight departure from the rule which governs, and the chancellor of that time was severely criticized for the action he had taken. It is also true that in this country there has been a very great deal of criticism with respect to judicial appointments because it has been felt in few cases has the test been the merit of the appointee. To get away from that in a new democracy is not an easy thing. No one knows the difficulty better than I. Under those circumstances I think we must continue to try to secure the best available material because I still hold that of the three branches of government the judicial is the most important. This legislative branch can undo to-morrow what it has done to-day, and it frequently does-although it does not do it so quickly as to-day and tomorrow. The executive charged with its responsibility also may change and undo what has been done. The judicial branch, if it follows the common law system by which precedents, that is the decisions of the courts,, are binding upon inferior courts, cannot readily undo to-morrow what has been done to-day. One of the great poets of;the Victorian era, the poet laureate, made some observations touching these myriads of precedents which have so great an apparent effect upon the minds of men, and so govern the administration of justice, these precedents, these decisions, these judicial interpretations, these determine what the language of a statute really means.
For instance, to-day we pass a statute which may seem very clear to some hon. members. They may have no difficulty in understanding *what it means, but in the end the judges of this country must be able, without the aid of Hansard-because the courts have ruled that Hansard cannot be referred to in the courts to ascertain the intention of the legislature. The intention of a legislature as expressed in words in debate has no effect, but the intention as manifested by the language employed and interpreted in the light of preceding decisions must determine what the legislature meant.

Let us for example consider the two words "trade" and "commerce" which appear in subsection 2 of section 91 of the British North America Act. When the case of Parsons versus the Queen went to the privy council the interpretation of the words trade and commerce had to be considered. It was found that the meaning of the words trade and commerce had been determined in a statute passed in the reign of Queen Anne. There hon. members have a precedent indicating the power and strength of a judicial decision applied to an act passed in 1867, where words similar to those used in that act had been used in the days of Queen Anne and had been given a particular meaning which governed the interpretation of an act passed in 1867. Thus in our courts we find that where similar words are employed in statutes and they have already been judicially interpreted, that interpretation continues.
So under those circumstances, in this highly developed civilization, the demand for highly trained minds becomes greater. The compensation which men of our profession receive for the services they render to-day are, some people think, out of all proportion to the actual value of the services. I think possibly the complaint is not wholly unfounded. I think it may not be untruly said that perhaps some members of our profession are more highly paid than they should be; that may well be said. It must also be realized, however, that in the hands of the members of our profession there rests a tremendous responsibility, and that no consideration of fear, favour or affection must govern them in the discharge of their duty. From that body, from the legal profession, must be recruited the bench. That is why I take it the ex-Minister of Justice has very properly said we are so desirous of maintaining the standards in the legal profession, because those standards are reflected in those obtaining on the bench.
The salaries paid to members of the bench are wholly inadequate-wholly inadequate. They do not attract to the bench the best minds. However, as the ex-minister has said there is never a dearth of candidates for judicial office. It is remarkable that while salaries are poor, the remuneration small compared with what they might have received from practising their profession, the sense of security and dignity, and the certainty of a retiring allowance will attract men to the bench.
Having in mind the great traditions of the legal profession, the fine traditions of the bench, the services it had rendered to man-

kind, the services it had rendered in Canada in the interpretation of our constitution and the determination of justice between contending parties, as well as the administration of our criminal laws, it is not unfair, is it, to think that with that security, that dignity and that retiring allowance they should make for this year a contribution in keeping with that made by their fellows of the state? I certainly feel, probably more strongly than hon. members opposite, that their salaries must not be touched. In my judgment their salaries could not be decreased but they could be increased. However when it came to a question of making a contribution when others had done so and were doing so, when others had offered to do so and were doing so, in order that there might be no invidious distinctions or that we might not create differences or, shall I say, unfair criticism, making it difficult for two members of the same bench to discuss questions with one another without one thinking that the other was endeavouring to enhance his own position at the expense of the other, we, by the exercise of power conferred upon us by statute, to raise money by taxation, are imposing that tax upon the judicial class, the bench, upon army, navy and police officers, the last three having offered voluntarily to have the deduction made from their salaries. How can it be said that that is discriminatory legislation any more than it could be said if I imposed a tax upon any man who went into a theatre to-night; certainly, he who goes into the theatre pays it. He who does not, does not. You discriminate, certainly, against the man who attends the theatre, and you collect from him a tax. You collect none from the man who does not go to the theatre. So far as that is concerned, the man who occupies a position on the bench contributes ten per cent, and he who does not does not.
I was rather surprised to hear the exMinister of Justice suggest that the principle of taxation without representation had any application here. Taxation without representation never applied to individuals or their avocations. If so the form of government that has been commended so strongly at times in the province of Alberta would have its justification, for then indeed you would have to have a class government in which every class would be represented. The House of Commons would not be complete, in such case, if every class, every occupation and profession did not have here a representative. That is not taxation without representation. Taxation without representation means that the great body of the people cannot be taxed

until that same great body of people has the right and opportunity to express themselves through their representative.
This House of Commons reflects the whole opinion of the nation not any part of it. It reflects every vocation and every profession, and not any one of them; it reflects them all. The minute this parliament passes any taxing law, that minute it exercises the power reposed in it by the whole body of the nation. The old philosophic principle as to how the rule of majorities came into being finds expression there, and once the majority has acted then the statute is a statute of the Canadian people, and not of one party or of a majority in the house. So all the people find representation through that 'tradition which goes back at least six hundred or seven hundred years as to the rule of majorities and which has been discussed in so scholarly a manner by one of the members of our profession who investigated the foundations of our institutions.
Now, I think on sober reflection it will be found that .most of the members of the judiciary, ill-paid though they are, will realize, and gladly realize, that this affords to them an opportunity, not to render to Caesar what is due to Caesar, but by the application of a law to every member of the judiciary, and alike to .every member of the military, to make that contribution which is made by members of the public service,. That is what is aimed at, that is what is secured. I have no doubt as to the validity of the power, I have no doubt as to the completeness of the authority, that rests upon this parliament to do it.
As to the propriety of .it, as I have said, there seems to be no doubt when all in three classes, and substantial numbers in the other, have expressed not only willingness buit an earnest desire that they might be able to participate in the work of rehabilitation in this period of depression by making their contribution to the revenues of Canada. It is in that sense and for that purpose that this legislation is submitted. Had it not been felt as strongly as we can feel any matter that could be established by reason of our conviction as to its soundness, that to reduce salaries would be a wholly improper exercise of power and a,n invasion of the independence of the judiciary, we would have dealt with them as the other members have been dealt with.
One word more as to the office of lieutenant-governor. I will not traverse the ground I dealt with the other evening, but I have received at least one communication from a lieutenant-governor saying he would have 41761-189
to leave his position even if this ten per cent reduction were made, for the reason, as the ex-Minister of Justice has said, that the salaries .provided for lieutenant-governors are the salaries provided in 1867, or later in the case of the newer provinces; none of them bear any relation to the cost and expense of maintaining the office. I know of no lieutenant-governor with whom I have had any conversation or discussion who at the end of his term of office has not found himself indebted to his own private means for some sum, sometimes small, sometimes large, depending upon his sense of obligation with respect to the hospitality he dispenses.
With regard to pensions, these are not reduced by this legislation. Pensions are a matter of contract. To reduce a pension would violate the condition which I referred to a moment ago. There is the case to which the member for Antigonish-Guysborough referred, and which is within the memory of some members of this house, where we were unable to secure a chairman for the pensions appeal court. There are members in this house who might have filled that position if they so desired, but the salary was so inadequate that they would not leave their professional activities for the purpose. Some suggested that a salary of less than $1,000 a month would be wholly inadequate. We had to find a judge, not sixty years of age, who had served fifteen years so as not to sacrifice his retiring allowance, and who would be willing to serve in that difficult position. If I say we went over the entire list from one end of the country to the other and ultimately secured the gentleman of whom the member for Antigonish-Guysborough has spoken, I state the fact was known to most of us. I know that when the hon. gentleman said that a retired judge who had accepted a lieutenant-governship received his pension last year, he must have realized that that retired judge received his pension up to the time he was appointed lieutenant-governor. For my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Justice will realize that in the case of the lieutenant-governor of Saskatchewan it was determined that on a true construction of the statute he was not entitled to receive a retiring allowance while acting as lieutenant-governor; and the successors of the former lieutenant-governor of Alberta as well as of Quebec, who occupied seats on the bench, at once ceased to draw any retiring allowance by virtue of having accepted those positions under the crown. Therefore so far as they are concerned they have received no retiring allowance since they were appointed lieutenant-governors. There are members of the house receiving substantial pensions, for

services rendered to the state. No one suggests for a moment that there should be any deduction from those pensions. They had a right under the statute, if for ill-health or otherwise, on a proper compliance with the terms of the law to receive a pension of maybe $3,000, $4,000, $5,000 or $6,000 per annum. They pay income tax upon their pensions. Their pension is part of their income together with their sessional indemnity. But to reduce that pension thus earned is to interfere with an executed contract; for the contract was executed when the term of service called for by the statute had been ended and the right to the emolument completed.
That is all I have to observe with respect to this matter. This means simply that when a farmer goes to buy a set of harness, he will have to pay the increased price for it, because, let me emphasize again, the best harness, sole and belting leathers are made from hides that have been imported from the Argentine, Uruguay, the southern states, and not from hides produced in Canada. Unquestionably the result of this verbal understanding that the minister had with New Zealand, that on his return to Canada he should have a tariff put upon hides, has landed us in this position: we do not benefit the farmer who sells hides, because

the price of the class of hides that he produces will not be affected a particle, and we compel the tanner to pay a higher price for the hides he uses. He will recoup himself by charging the local consumer a higher price for harness leather. He also will be handicapped in the export market. That is a very striking illustration, Mr. Chairman, of the effect of interfering unduly with the course of trade. In this case it is of no benefit to ourselves; it is an injury to the tanner and an injury to the country to have this very valuable trade interfered with.
There is another point I should like to emphasize at this moment, and perhaps it has a bearing on the principles that will be followed at the coming Imperial conference. Evidently our Minister of Trade and Commerce came to a verbal understanding with the representatives of New Zealand that he would come back home and have a duty imposed on hides. It is a very serious thing if in our trade agreements we allow a country with which we are dealing to insist that we shall alter our own tariff. Let us give them whatever advantages of our tariffs we have to offer, but I say it is pretty serious if we are to accept dictation from outside as to what we shall do with our own tariff. That was just the mistake which the Prime Minister made when he went over to England last year. We on this side have always taken the position that we were content to take whatever preferences the British people offered us in their markets, but we absolutely refused to interfere with the business of the United Kingdom and to say what they should do with regard to their tariff. It is true, I know, that the Liberal government in making the agreement with Australia did adopt that principle with reference to raisins, but it must be remembered that the duty on raisins was not in any sense a protective tariff, but entirely a revenue tariff. I want to insist that if there is any disposition to allow other nations to say what our tariff shall be, we are heading straight for disaster. We can never hope to build up a united empire that way. We can only hope to build up a united empire by each country within the empire retaining complete freedom in the making of its own tariffs. I think I have shown quite conclusively, Mr. Chairman, that the result of this verbal agreement which the Minister of Trade and Commerce made with New Zealand and which the government now seeks to put into effect-I suppose it will have to be done in order to keep faith with New Zealand-cannot be anything else but bad both for the tanners and for the Canadian producer of hides.

I think the hon. member for Lisgar is entirely off the track in talking like that. There is practically no market for hides in this country. The hon. member says it will not benefit the farmer. What is he going to do with his hides? Is he going to bury them? What is the reason for hides being the price they are to-day? The hon. member is talking about prices of hides three or four years ago. Does he not know that hides are not worth anything to-day? He is off the track entirely.

The arguments which I combated in 1926 and 1929 were the same arguments which hon. gentlemen are using to-day when hides are worth almost nothing as compared with twenty cents a pound a few years ago.
They are not using hides at all of the type my hon. friend was speaking about.

Is it not a fact that some of the large tanneries in Canada do not use a pound of Canadian hides? But, generally speaking, the tanneries are using a certain proportion of our own hides and will continue to do so under any circumstances. I think, Mr. Chairman, that when the argument I have used is given consideration it will be found that it is perfectly valid.

This is one time I find myself in agreement with the hon. member for Lisgar. I do not want to do anything to raise the price of harness leather or of harness to the farmer in western Canada, because the farmer in western Canada is going back to horses; he is tired of the tractor. The hon. member for Lisgar is quite right in his statement with reference to hides. I put some money into a tannery in Winnipeg and tried to tan hides. I do not forget it and I shall not forget it for some time. The hides in Canada are not suitable for harness leather. My hon. friend is quite correct in that statement. If they were, why does the Lang Tanning Company in Kitchener go to South America and the United States for their raw hides for making harness leather? The hides we have in Canada, unfortunately, are covered with barbed wire scratches. Any man who puts his money into a tannery in Canada-and there have been two of us in Winnipeg-will soon learn from experience. I am totally in agreement with what the hon. member for Lisgar has said with regard to hides, and I do trust that something will be done so that the price of harness leather and the tariff on hides entering Canada will not be raised because, as I said, Mr. Chairman, the farmers are going

oack to horses. I am sorry that a good many of my friends on this side will not agree with me, but I felt it necessary to support the statement of the hon. member for Lisgar. I listened very closely to what he said, and he was quite correct in his statement.

As one who comes from the city'-which is the home of perhaps the largest tannery in the British Empire and of still another tannery of very considerable size, I might say a word with regard to this matter.
In the first place I will admit that in any treaty, and this provision is the result of a treaty with New Zealand, there must be give and take. If the New Zealand producer of hides would benefit by the imposition of this fifteen per cent duty it would be an argument for it, but I am told, and I think correctly, that New Zealand hides are not suited for the making of harness leather or of sole leather either. If this provision helped the Canadian producer of hides it would be an (argument for it, but the same thing applies to Canadian hides as applies to New Zealand hides. They are not suitable for making the kind of leather of which we are speaking.
Something has been said as to the export trade in leather. My hon. friend from Lisgar stated that if it is true that the duty of fifteen per cent must be paid on these hides that are imported from the Argentine-the Lang Tanning Company at Kitchener and I believe all the Canadian tanneries import their hides from the Argentine-it must necessarily increase the cost of producing leather, and thus make it more difficult to compete with other countries in the export market for leather.

fMr. Mullins.]
in error, by an hon. member on this side of the house. I understand the export business in leather has been practically cut off because of tariffs in other countries being increased, and it is no longer possible to send leather to other countries.
The only point I wish to make is this: The imposition of the duty will no doubt increase the production costs of leather. The tanner will reimburse himself by increasing the price of the leather to the consumer in Canada. If you were going to get some benefit out of it by. helping the New Zealand producer of hides, or if you would help the Canadian producer of hides, then I would say there is an argument for the duty. As I see it, however, the only possible benefit that can come to Canadians is by way of added revenue on hides imported from the Argentine-because they will still be imported from that country. The only benefit which will come to Canadians will be through the increased revenue brought about by the imposition of a duty of fifteen per cent. Against that we must set this: It increases the cost of leather to the Canadian consumer.
In that connection I should like to say a few words in regard to the contention of the hon. member for Marquette. It is perfectly true there has been an increase in the production of harness leather. The Lang Tanning Company of Kitchener was mentioned, and may I say that they are producers of sole and harness leather. At one time they produced only harness leather, and then owing to the fact that the horse has almost disappeared they became tanners of sole leather. I am told that within the last few months they have had great increases in the sale of harness leather to western Canada. The farmers of western Canada, for reasons of their own,-perhaps because they cannot afford to use tractors, or because of the high price of gasoline,

have gone back to the use of horses, involving the use of harness leather. As a result the business of tanning harness leather in the city of Kitchener has been stimulated. What will come out of this legislation would be an increased price of harness leather to the farmers in western Canada.
I do not see any corresponding value, except through added revenue. If this is a measure for the production of revenue, I can see no other arguments.

Is it not possible the Argentine will reduce its prices to meet competition? That is invariably the case.
