New York acts as a sort of free port zone for merchandise destined for Canada. As I indicated the other day, this very important item of trade accrues to the credit of the United States so far as the Argentine is concerned, and Canada gets no credit for it at all. My own opinion is that it is highly desirable to ensure the movement of trade directly from the country of origin to Canada, if it is possible to do so, because it will give to us in that market an enhanced credit, which will enable us in turn to sell our goods there. I am now dealing with the broad general principle, which I think ought not to be lost sight of.
Now, it has been alleged that we do not produce hides which are required by the tanneries for certain purposes, such as harness leather, sole leather, and so forth. I think undue weight is given to that statement. In part it is quite accurate, but to say we can get no hides in Canada suitable for those purposes is not a fair statement. It is, however, a fact that the producers of raw hides in Canada have not developed as good a system of sorting and marketing as characterizes, for instance, the New York or the Argentine market; and there can be no doubt that so far as the Argentine producers are concerned they have a more uniform production of hides of a certain type and class.
I have received quite a number of criticisms from producers of hides in this country that in the negotiation of the New Zealand treaty we were not looking after their interests sufficiently in leaving hides on the free list. It has been argued that by leaving hides from New Zealand free, and by having the British

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
preference free also, we are doing something to affect prejudicially the producers of hides in Canada. It is true that the tanneries, though I cannot say I have received representations other than one or two very moderate letters, may think they have cause for complaint in the fact that we are imposing duties of 10 per cent and 15 per cent under the intermediate and general tariffs. In the first place I submit to the house that there is a general system of dumping going on the world over. Many countries are practising dumping in a manner that has never been witnessed before, I suppose, in the'history of external trade; they are exceedingly anxious to develop their exports, to correct adverse balances of trade and also to bolster up their own exchange by increasing exports. The result is that with the low prices of commodities there is a tendency to disregard almost entirely home values and to export goods at almost any figure procurable. I have not under my hand the present day prices of hides, but I know they are exceedingly low. A few days ago, if my memory serves me aright, I saw quotations as low as two cents a pound, and I understand that Canadian producers-I will not say farmers, because probably they would get even less-are being paid from one cent to one and one-half cents per pound by the dealers. Obviously a duty of 10 per cent or 15 per cent on hides, with the present condition of the market, is not going to affect the leather situation to any extent at all. The effect would be so small upon the finished product that it would not be noticeable.
What authority has the minister for that statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
My authority is the
figure to which I have referred, the very low price of the commodity, which is unquestionably below anything that might be considered the cost price of this article.
If the duty is so small that it will not make any difference, will it not be futile and useless?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The duty is imposed as
one of the conditions of the negotiation of the treaty. My point is that the treaty is for a year. The New Zealanders will be here in July and August, I suppose, at the Imperial conference, and during that period we intend to discuss with them the terms of the treaty and the possibility of its extension beyond the period of a year. As a result of the conference we hope that such matters as are outstanding, which may present some difficulties at the present time, may be finally determined.
[Mr. Stevens.!
My submission to the committee is that under existing conditions, with the present low price of the commodity, the duty imposed is not going to seriously affect the business. In the second place, it must be borne in mind that there is a very substantial duty on leather goods. I have the rate under my hand but had not time to look it up before I rose to speak. At any rate there is a very substantial protection with regard to the finished article, and the added value that goes into the finishing of these hides in the form in which they are marketed so greatly exceeds the cost of the raw material that the ad valorem rate of duty will not affect the finished article to any great extent. Unquestionably it will affect it to a degree, but one must keep in mind the relative values of these different commodities.
I should like now to say a word to the hon. member for Lisgar, who referred to this as a case of another country dictating our tariff. That is not so. In any negotiations looking to a treaty there are bound to arise conditions which call for changes, amendments or adjustments in existing tariff rates. This is one of the items which called for an adjustment, just as on the other hand I think there were one or two items in connection with which New Zealand would have to amend its tariff to meet the conditions of the treaty.
My hon. friend across the way asked if I had given the matter any thought. I can assure him that I have given the matter a great deal of thought. It would not serve any purpose to now go through all the processes of thinking-

I do not think my hon.
friend caught my question. I did not suggest that he had not been thinking; I wanted to know if he had taken any steps to assure himself that the New Zealand or Canadian hides would fill the place of the Argentine hides which it is now intended to replace.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
My own opinion, if it
is worth anything, is that to a certain degree Canadian hides may meet the requirements of the tanneries.
They may?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Let me make that point
quite clear. I do not say for a moment that they will fully meet those requirements, but I want to point out to the committee that it has always been the practice of any industry which has established certain contacts for its materials to emphasize the difficulties imposed far beyond the actual burden, when anything is done to interfere with the normal routine

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
of their business. That is almost axiomatic; you find it in every case, and I have never seen it fail. The moment you interfere with the ordinary practice of private industries an extreme interpretation is placed upon the difficulty which is thus imposed. I do not think the interference with the business of the tanneries will be a matter of very great significance, and I think in part they will be able to secure, from the existing supplies of hides in Canada, materials that will serve their purposes, but not as conveniently, not so well assorted, not marketed in such large quantities as is the case in New York, where they are well graded and readily available. To a degree, however, I think hides from other countries can be replaced by Canadian hides, and to a degree also by Australian and New Zealand hides. This should give Great Britain a chance to market some green hides here-not that I think Great Britain is a producer of hides, but she certainly is just as good an assembler of hides as New York is, and I see no reason why she should not get a share of the business. Perhaps I ought not to say this, but I will take a chance

I think an opportunity is being afforded of opening up negotiations with the Argentine which may bring about distinctly advantageous results. Trade relations between Canada and the Argentine certainly have to be improved. There is an excellent market in that country for a wide range of manufactured articles from Canada, and we can buy but little in return, but one product which we can buy is hides. I see no reason why there should not be some arrangement entered into with that country. As far as certain classes of hides are concerned, New Zealand will have a distinct advantage, and that is what we expect and desire.

In the event of Great Britain becoming an assembler of hides, would that automatically do away with the tariff now prevailing against those hides which may be gathered together in Great Britain and then shipped to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I think it is open for us to deal with that matter should it arise.

Coming as I do from a riding in which is located the largest tannery of sole leather in the British Empire, I think I should say something in this regard. There are two lines of thought in this matter, one academic and the other practical. The minister has a laudable object in view when he desires to transfer to New Zealand the business in hides, but he may not be aware of
the fact that this is practically impossible. New Zealand hides are useless for the manufacture of sole leather. They are largely cow hides; they are thin and will not make good sole leather. The market for hides is not in New York, as the minister says, but in Chicago and the Argentine. I refer now to that market outside of the local domestic market. Under this treaty duties of ten and fifteen per cent are being placed upon the raw material for the manufacture of sole leather. How can this country go out into the markets of the world and compete with England and every other country, with the exception of the United States, where hides are allowed to enter free? A handicap of fifteen per cent is being placed upon the tanneries of this country. I am credibly informed that if things stay as they are, eveiy sole leather tannery in this country will be put out of business. The minister speaks lightly about this matter, but my information is that a duty of seven and a half per cent will be required on manufactured leather to equal this duty of fifteen per cent on the raw material. The manufacturers of sole leather in this country are taking all the hides that are available in Canada, and would take hides from New Zealand if good sole leather could lbe made from them, but that cannot be done. Something is being done in connection with this industry which has never been done with any other-a duty is being placed on its raw material.
I think I have a right to protest against the putting out of business of any industry, especially one located in my own riding. That is what this treaty is going to do should it go through in its present form. England allows hides to enter free and she is our main competitor in the world market. How are we to compete with England when a duty of fifteen per cent is being placed upon the raw material? There are only two courses open; either more protection must be given to the finished article, or an additional cost must be placed upon the consumers of this country. I contend that both these methods would be wrong. I tell the minister quite frankly that he is absolutely on the wrong track. If good sole leather could be made out of New Zealand hides, they could have been used in the past. The tanneries are scouring the earth for hides; they are bringing them from China and Japan, but the principal market is in Chicago and the Argentine. The hides obtained from those markets are the only ones that will make first class sole leather. New Zealand hides will not do it. I object to the way this treaty was born and the way it was put through the house. Men have spent their time and

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
money during the past fifty or seventy-five years in building up this industry, and for a number of years they have been operating at an actual monetary loss in order to keep going; then the government comes along and puts duties of ten and fifteen per cent on their raw material. I protest against the whole thing; it was wrong in its conception and it is wrong in its application.
What about the Canadian producer?

The tanneries have
taken every Canadian hide available. The only people to be affected by this treaty will be the packers. They have been withdrawing their hides from the market ever since the treaty was announced. They are the ones who will benefit, not the farmers who are producing hides.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Weyburn put a question, and at the moment I had not the record before me. If he will look at section 286 of the Customs Act, chapter 42 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, he will find the drawback.

Has the minister answered
the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario?

In view of the speech that the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has made, I should like to say a word. I am delighted to hear him speak as he has done; it gives us some reason to believe the gospel we have been trying to preach for the last six or seven years is beginning to be accepted. If I remember aright, the hon. member was one of those who in 1926 made a speech which moved me to speak as I did in the address that I quoted this afternoon.
Never in my life did I advocate a duty on raw material.

I am well aware that on
the general question of duties the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario spoke of the tanneries that were going out of business. I am sorry for the ^Minister of Trade and Commerce, because he certainly laboured hard when he was endeavouring to show why this proposal should be endorsed. He did not speak with his usual fluency and authority. He spoke of the possibility of Great Britain becoming an assembling place for hides. I presume the thought in his mind was that those hides would go there from the Argentine. I wonder how New Zealand would accept that way of getting around the agreement we have made-tfiat is, to have the 
hides shipped to Great Britain and thence to Canada. That would seem to be a method of getting around the agreement with New Zealand, but I cannot imagine how she would view it.
Mr. McGIBBON; Great Britain imports about seventy-five per cent of her hides.

I do not think we can emphasize too strongly the fact that our hides are suitable for certain purposes, and I believe they are used to the fullest extent possible for those purposes. In the figures I quoted this afternoon I mentioned that large quantities of upper leathers were imported. I imagine the greater portion of the upper leather in our ordinary shoes can be made from Canadian hides. But I want to point out that in constantly increasing ratio the cattle which are being slaughtered in Canada are the smaller ones. Even when Great Britain was taking a smaller steer than she is willing to take now, the large animals were going across the seas, and the reason our Canadian cattle are not suitable for the making of hides lies in the fact that the great bulk of our cattle slaughtered here are small ones that do not produce heavy hides, so that what they produce is not suitable for our tanners who have been buying from the Argentine. There is reason to believe that NevTZealand hides are of the same quality. New Zealand is not a beef country, as the Argentine is; she is a dairy countiy, and there is no reason to suppose the qualities of New Zealand hides are in any degree different from our own. The probability is that they are in the same class, and they will not replace the hides which we have been getting from other countries.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce, in answering my question as to what assurance he had that our hides or New Zealand hides would be satisfactory in place of those from South America, told us that the tanners or manufacturers were prone to exaggerate or over-emphasize the difficulty that any change such as this would make in their operations. He thinks the Canadian hides may be satisfactory and may not interfere very seriously with the business of the tanners. Because he holds the opinion they may not make very much difference, he feels justified in playing with the tanners, as it were, throwing difficulties in their way and telling them they had better overcome them. As regards the question of insisting on direct shipment from the Argentine to Canada instead of the Argentine hides being bought on the Chicago market, if our manufacturers buy hides in Chicago there must be a reason for their

Ways-and Means-Customs Tariff
doing so. If it would pay them to import the hides directly from Argentina, that is what they would surely do. It must be more profitable for them to buy their hides in Chicago.

They buy them both
ways.

I have no doubt the reason is that, Chicago being an assembling place for hides of all kinds, the buyers have a greater opportunity there to select what they want. If you impose customs duties which make that impossible, you put upon the Canadian tanner the necessity of sending somebody to Argentina to pick up the hides, thus rendering his business more expensive. In regard to the duty being only 15 per cent and the hides only one-half cent per pound, it is said that this will not amount to very much. I suppose 15 per cent of nothing is nothing, but hides are not going to remain at that price. What will happen when the price advances?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Ten per cent from Argentina.
I might inform the hon. member that the duty to-day is equal to seven and a half per cent on the cost of the finished product.

As the price of the raw
hide advances, it will be still more. To my mind the most amazing statement which the minister made was that by this treaty he hoped to divert to New Zealand the trade which we have now with Argentina. Then he hopes to enter into another treaty with Argentina to switch the trade back again. Surely this ought to be a lesson to us or our government as to what they should or should not do at the Imperial conference. In this we see the direct result of an attempt to divert trade. It is much easier to kill than to divert trade. We are putting obstacles in the way of our trade with Argentina in the hope that that trade will switch to New Zealand. The result will be that we shall lose the trade entirely. This should be a warning to the government to do nothing at the Imperial conference to try to build up empire trade by putting obstacles in. the way of trade outside the empire. You can very seldom divert trade, but you can always kill it.

I do not wish in any way to embarrass the minister by opposing this resolution. A few days ago, speaking on the New Zealand , treaty, I was able to compliment the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the
treaty which he had made with New Zealand, but on that occasion, due to the faot that I had not had time to study the New Zealand treaty, I had no knowledge that it was the intention of the minister to introduce a budget resolution making a duty applicable to hides from Argentina and other countries. I think some remarks which were made this afternoon and this evening with regard to the injury which would be done to the Canadian hide business were made because there was not a complete understanding of the difference between Argentine and Canadian hides. If hon. members will just realize that there is no other country in the world producing beef cattle as large or as uniform in size as the j Argentine; that in that country barbed wire is not permitted for fencing; that there are no jvaitdedlies or insects which destroy a hide, and that probably the hides of Argentine steers

ire taken off by as expert abattoir workers as there are in the world, they will appreciate why fior-size and freedom from defect, for weight and quality, the Argentine hide has become the accepted hide in the world's sole and harness leather business. Our Canadian tanneries have developed from very small industries using domestic hides. The Lang Tanning Company in the city of Kitchener, to which the hon. member for North Waterloo referred, is the last of thirty-seven tanneries formerly operating in that county. This industry has developed into the largest tannery in the British Empire, under free trade with the various countries of the world on leather and hides. Therefore, given free trade, our Canadian tanners have held their own in producing harness and sole leather with the tanners of other countries. True, Canada imports certain fine leather for shoes and upholstering, but speaking broadly Canada has gained very much by the tanning here of foreign hides. Before anything is done which will interfere with the price of raw material required for the foreign or domestic leather trade, a great deal of consideration should be given to the subject. I quite realize that the minister in making his treaty with New Zealand encountered a lot of difficulties, and I quite sympathize with him in those difficulties. But what has been said by my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario with regard to the suitability of New Zealand hides for making sole leather is absolutely correct, and I am assured by those engaged in tanning harness and sole leather that it is utterly impossible to make the type of sole leather, from the hide of a dairy cow that would be suitable for the markets of the world.	,

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
There are two phases of this situation. One the member for North Waterloo in a very few words ably pointed out to the minister, namely that he had to choose between one of these two things:	He would derive a certain revenue by applying this duty on hides, but he had inevitably to face higher prices on harness and sole leather to the consumers in Canada. That phase is of interest. My hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario is interested in an entirely different phase. He is interested in whether the producers of sole leather in Canada are going to be able to hold the Canadian market. They will now have to pay duty on hides from the Argentine, the very type of hide that is wanted, and the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario is interested to know whether the Argentine hide tanned in Great Britain into sole leather is to be permitted to enter Canada free. If that is to be the case, and sole leather is to enter Canada free of duty, then of course the whole market will be lost to the Canadian tanner. If, on the other hand, the minister is prepared to give the Canadian tanner what he considers an adequate tariff on sole leather from Great Britain, that adequate tariff must be added to the cost of sole leather to the consumer in Canada, and we revert once more to the position put by the hon. member for North Waterloo, that the ultimate cost of this duty is going to be on the consumer of sole leather in Canada.
The hon. member for Marquette raised a point of very great interest this afternoon. It is impossible to make from Canadian hides the type of harness leather required. You cannot get the lengths of cut required, and Canadian hides are of poor quality, with too many scratches, too many tears and too many cuts. They are not the type of hide that tans easily. The tanner has certain operations through which he must go, and a vat full of poor hides takes just as much time to handle and uses just as much liquid in the tanning as a vat full of good hides, so it is only natural that the tanner desirous of making a profit on his industry wants to start with raw material of the highest quality and that will give him the smallest percentage of waste. So even if Canadian hides are used to as great an extent as they can be used, there are certain types of leather which cannot well be made from them, and the whole market, domestic and foreign, for certain types of leather will be lost to the Canadian producer unless the proper type of hide is used.
There is another feature which I believe is of just as great importance as anything

else, and that is the question to which the minister has referred. There are not many commodities that we can buy from the Argentine republic. The Argentine republic has been one of Canada's very good customers, and if the spirit of this treaty is to destroy our market in the Argentine the reflex loss through the treaty will be more disastrous to us than any advantages that may otherwise accrue from it. Like my hon. friend from Weybum I simply cannot understand the minister's remark that having negotiated this treaty with New Zealand he proposes to use it as a club over the Argentine to make a more satisfactory treaty with that country. We have already a trade with the Argentine which is tremendously favourable to this dominion, and I would be very loath indeed to disturb this trade, particularly when the balance is very much in our favour, and particularly when the Argentine supplies us with a commodity which our manufacturers require. I quite realize the desire of New Zealand to market a lot of hides, but I am going to say to the minister that I am told by those who know whereof they speak that New Zealand is simply not able to supply Canada with enough hides to replace the hides now coming in from the Argentine republic. I am told that the tanners are willing to do everything they possibly can to increase the use of New Zealand and Australian hides, but they do not want to be deprived of securing the class of hides which they really require in their business.
I know that in dealing with the New Zealand government the minister unquestionably had so many items to consider that it would be physically impossible, without an unusual amount of advice on every subject, to know all that should be known in negotiations of this kind. I am not blaming the minister if on some small points of the treaty he was not able to present the viewpoint of those affected as fully as he might be expeoted to do. I believe he has not given this question of hides his usual careful thought, otherwise this part of the treaty would not be under discussion in the parliament of Canada to-night. None of us on this side of the house wants to oppose a treaty within the empire, a treaty which is replacing an old treaty. Some items in the new treaty I do not think are as desirable as what the old treaty contained; other items may be more desirable, but here is an item in which the very boast of my hon. friend's party is being neglected entirely. My hon. friend's party has always said:	We are
going to better conditions in Canada by helping industry and creating employment. If

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
this item does what the tanners of Canada think it is going to do, it will eventually cause serious unemployment. There can be no question about that. My hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario, who is noted for his loyalty to his party, and a man whom his party should be proud to number in its ranks, is certainly not standing in this house and warning the minister against the terms of this treaty without first having given the matter very serious consideration. My hon. friend from Marquette, who has had practical experience in starting a tannery and losing money trying to run it, is not warning the minister without very serious consideration. I would strongly advise the Minister of Finance to pass on to some other resolution and hold this item up until a little more thought is given to it and he has considered further whether he really wants it to pass.

It gives one considerable satisfaction to hear the expressions of opinion of the two hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house who have spoken in defence of the principle of allowing raw products to enter Canada free. I always had the idea that although the Conservative party was strong for protection on finished products it had a leaning towards the free entry of raw products. But apparently they have gone back on their principles on this occasion, and we have the spectacle to-night of the Conservative party, by putting a duty on raw materials, doing an injury to industry, which they have avowedly set out to protect by way of high tariffs. What I wish to protest against, and protest vigorously, is that tariffs inevitably force the consumer in the country by which they are imposed to pay a higher price for the commodities that are manufactured therein. Without going at length into the argument presented by hon. gentlemen on this side and by the two hon. gentlemen opposite, I want to express my very strong disapproval of any attempt to impose tariffs on raw materials, above all things. That I think is a principle which no party in Canada should uphold for a minute. While I say that, I am just as strongly opposed to excessive tariffs upon finished products, because they are bringing the inevitable result. We see distress not only among our rural population but among our manufacturers, and that condition has been brought about by the policy of this government. As long as the Conservative party continues to follow that policy, just so long will we in Canada be in our present condition.

Mr. Chairman, when on the advice of some westerners I attempted to operate a tannery in western Canada, I found it necessary to go to Mr. Lang, ask him to
go over my plant, and tell me where my difficulties arose. When he came into the plant and looked at the hides I was attempting to tan he said. "There is where you are wrong; you cannot make harness leather out of that type of hides. You have to get your hides from warm countries where they are thin, where they do not carry too much hair, and where they are not harmed by barbed wire scratches or branding." I made harness leather, and before I put it on the market I tested it. I wanted to know that I was putting out a good product, and with that in mind I took a pair of traces, or tugs as some people call them, down to the lumber yard and hitched them to a load of lumber. I am speaking of John Arbuthnot's yard on Princess street; no doubt the hon. member for Lisgar knows where it is. I want to say to hon. members that after the first pull the horses gave the load of lumber the pole fell down. You cannot get the stretch out of small hides. That is practical information, and I want the committee to know it. I paid for that experience. You cannot get the stretch out of the smaller hides that you can get out of those big spready hides from the warm countries. If the government does anything to increase the price of harness it is making a mistake. I do not want the price of harness raised, and from this seat I shall voice my opposition to any measure which will affect detrimentally the farmers in western Canada. I came here with the distinct understanding that any tariffs we imposed or any action we took would not raise the price of commodities to the consumer. I am not going to sit in this committee and support any measure which will raise those prices. If this measure passes I fear that the price of harness may increase. As I said before, the farmers in western Canada are coming back to the use of horses and for those horses they need harness.
For years the Lang people have told me that there is only one place to get these large eighty pound spready hides, and that is in warm climates. They have several stacks of hides in their packing plants, and if an hon. member visited them to-day he would find that Canada, in producing what is known as baby beef, is producing a small hide which is not suitable for harness leather, and is hardly suitable for sole leather. What would hon. members do with a hide covered with brands? What would they make out of it? What could any hon. member manufacture out of such hides? It is absolutely impracticable to make harness leather from the

W7ays and Means-Customs Tariff
hides of our Canadian cattle, especially when we are raising small cattle and producing small hides. Before placing any duty upon hides which would affect the farmers of western Canada, I should like the minister to reconsider the matter.

What does the hon. member mean when he speaks of small cattle?
j Mr. MULLINS:	I am referring to hides
weighing from forty to sixty pounds. Sole leather cannot be manufactured from forty or sixty pound hides. If I were to go further into the matter I might state that leather cannot be made from inferior hides, and if my hon. friend thinks it can he ought to try it. When I began operations in the tannery I hung out a sign

the hon. member for St. Boniface knows all about it-that I was in the market to buy hides. They fired them at me from all parts of the west. Those hides were frozen, and when I thawed them out I found inside of the bundles feet cut off at the joints, and horns, and I can tell any hon. member in this committee that he cannot manufacture leather out of that type of raw material.

Mr. Chairman, I have had
no extensive experience as has my hon. friend from Marquette. He has been blaming the type of hides from which he had to manufacture, but probably he should have blamed the feet and horns that he found inside the bundle.
A moment ago I asked him as to what he termed a fair sized animal. I think my hon. friend will agree that the general run of cattle raised in Canada, outside of the baby beef referred to, average up pretty well. The steers shipped to the old country market last year received high praise. I cannot think that hides deteriorate to the extent described by hon. members. My father was a lumberman, and I can remember that the harness he used thirty or forty years ago was tanned and produced in Canada, made from the hides of Canadian cattle. In recent years I have not seen tugs W'hich wTould stand the strain that harness stood, and it is still in use. 1 can see no reason for discrediting Canadian hides, and I am convinced we are discriminating a little too much, and are showing a lack of confidence. May I say to my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario that to-day the farmers cannot sell their hides at any price. There has been a very strong suggestion that the tariff should be raised against foreign hides. Probably the tanners are not dealing as fairly as they might with the Canadian producer-
[DOT]"Mr. Mullins.]
and I may say there are no tanners in my constituency, or probably I would not talk so freely. In western Canada we cannot sell our hides; hon. members opposite know that to be a fact. There is a suggestion that our product is so inferior that it cannot be used for sole or harness leather, but I cannot believe that the majority of cattle produced in western Canada are inferior. They are first class cattle, and compare favourably with those from the Argentine or any other country.
Some reference has been made to climatic conditions. It seems to me that our climate should be conducive to the production of the best hides, despite the fact my hon. friend insists that the best can be produced only in warm climates. I can see no reason why, in the production of harness or sole leather, there should not be some protection so that we may use more hides produced in Canada.

Within the last hour I have received a letter from a manufacturer of rubber goods in Kitchener who formerly exported a very large quantity of his products to New Zealand. The business was cut off at the time the difficulty with New Zealand arose. Now he is very anxious to have the treaty go through because it will again stimulate the export of rubber goods. My correspondent encloses a letter from his agents in New Zealand, which reads as follows:
We have been informed by our minister

That is the New Zealand minister.
-that they are prepared to bring the treaty before parliament at any time. The delay is with your government.
That is the Canadian government.
We understand there is one item only in dispute. So we have again approached our government to agree to ratify exclusive of that item, if practicable.
I am curious to know if the minister is permitted to tell me whether that item might conceivably be hides; and, if so, whether there is not a possibility that it might be dropped from the tariff list.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Is the question directed to me?
Either to the Minister of Trade and Commerce or to the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have no knowledge, of course, of what the correspondent refers to, but certainly he does not refer to hides.

Mr. Chairman, at the time the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Loucks) went to western Canada that country was full

Special War Revenue Act
of steers weighing from 1,400 to 1,600 pounds apiece; to-day it is next to impossible to get that type of cattle. Their hides weighed eighty pounds apiece and would make harness leather; but to-day with the small cattle the hides are absolutely unsuitable for any tanner.

I move that item 599 be

Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Special War Revenue Act, chapter 179 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, as amended by chapter 50 of the statutes of 1928, chapter 57 of the statutes of 1929, chapter 43 of the statutes of 1930, and chapter 54 of the statutes of 1931, and to provide:-[DOT]
1.	(i) That every company authorized to
transact the business of insurance in Canada or in any province of Canada, other than life and marine insurance companies, fraternal benefit societies and purely mutual fire insurance companies insuring principally farm risks, shall pay for consolidated revenue fund tax of one per centum upon the net premiums received by the company in Canada on and after the first day of January, 1932.
(ii)	That every insurance company not so authorized to transact the business of insurance in Canada or in any province thereof but which maintains a deposit with the Minister of Finance as security for the claims of all Canadian policyholders exclusively of such company to the amount of at least the amount of the liabilities of the company to policyholders in Canada, shall pay for consolidated revenue fund a tax of one per centum upon the net premiums received by it in respect of insurance on property in Canada, other than marine insurance, effected or renewed in the portion of the calendar year 1932, and of each calendar year thereafter for which it maintains such deposit.
(iii)	That every person resident in Canada who insures or has insured his property situate in Canada, or any property situate in Canada in which he has an insurable interest other than that of an insurer of such property, with any British or foreign company or British or foreign underwriter or underwriters, or any association of persons,
(a) which, on the twenty-second day of October, 1931, had not a deposit with the Minister of Finance for the purpose and to the amount aforesaid, shall pay for consolidated revenue fund a tax of fifteen per centum of the gross premiums paid or payable by such person for such insurance during the year 1931; and a tax of five per centum of the total net cost to such person of such insurance effected or renewed in each of the calendar years 1921 to 1930, both inclusive, during which such company, underwriter or association did not maintain a deposit with the minister for the purpose and to the amount aforesaid, the amount of such tax payable in respect of any calendar year to be reduced by the amount of any tax heretofore paid to the minister in respect of such insurance for such calendar year; or

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: (b) which does not on or before the first day of May, 1932, or at the time such insurance is effected or renewed, if after the said date, maintain a deposit for the purpose and to the amount aforesaid, shall each year pay a tax of fifteen per centum of the gross premiums paid or payable for such insurance during the next preceding calendar year.
Has the minister the suggested amendment to be made to paragraph 1 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Paragraph 1 of the resolution will be amended by striking out the said paragraph and substituting the following:
1. (i) That every company authorized under the laws of the Dominion of Canada or of any province thereof to transact the business of insurance other than life and marine insurance companies, fraternal benefit societies, purely mutual fire insurance companies insuring principally farm risks, reciprocal insurance exchanges and mutual companies carrying on business on the premium deposit plan, shall pay for consolidated revenue fund a tax of one per centum upon the net premiums received by the company in Canada on and after the first day of January, 1932.
(ii)	That every mutual company authorized under the laws of the Dominion of Canada or of any province thereof to transact the business of insurance and which carries on business on the premium deposit plan and every reciprocal insurance exchange so authorized shall pay for consolidated revenue fund a tax of two per centum upon the net premiums received by it in Canada during the calendar year 1932 and each calendar year thereafter.
(iii)	That every person resident in Canada who insures or has insured his property situate in Canada, or any property situate in Canada in which he has an insurable interest other than that of an insurer of such property against risks other than marine risks, with any British or foreign company or any reciprocal insurance exchange which, on or before the first day of July, 1932, or at the time such insurance is effected or renewed if after the said date, is not authorized under the laws of the Dominion of Canada or of any province thereof to transact the business of insurance, shall pay for consolidated revenue fund a tax of fifteen per centum of the net premiums paid or payable for such insurance during the calendar year 1932 and each calendar year thereafter.
This is a complete change.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This amendment is in substance what was intended originally. The original resolution was prepared shortly before I delivered the budget speech and was not in conformity with the intention I had in mind at the time. This in effect means that if outside mutual companies attempt to do business in Canada without taking out registration or making a deposit either with the dominion or with the provinces, then in the event of an individual insisting upon effecting insurance with them he will pay a tax of 15 per cent upon the premiums; but if those mutual companies take out registration or make a deposit,

the tax is only two per cent. I would ask that the Minister of National Revenue move the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I move
the amendment as read by the Minister of Finance.

Do the mutuals pay twice
as high a tax as the standard companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. As a matter of fact
I think there is no exception taken to the two per cent tax, because, as my hon. friend knows, their premiums are based upon a different computation altogether. Furthermore, they have a class of risk on which there is an extremely low premium, and as a matter of fact the yield from this two per cent tax is relatively small. I may say that representations have been made to me that probably the tax ought to be considerably greater, but I understand that no exception has been taken even on the part of the mutual companies themselves.
There is no discrimination?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that question does not arise.
Is the retroactive feature still in the amendment which the minister proposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Has the minister any
estimate of the revenue which will be produced by these three provisions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is estimated that the
one per cent tax will yield about $1,000,000, while the total revenue from the two per cent tax will be very small, probably between $10,000 and $25,000. Any estimate of the revenue from the 15 per cent tax must be largely a glorified guess; it depends upon the extent to which those companies fail to avail themselves of the opportunity of registering either with the province or with the dominion. It will be only a fraction of the yield which will come from the one per cent tax.

I can be sure there is
no retroactive feature at all in the section now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, there is not.

I just want to make sure
whether or not I understood the minister with regard to these foreign mutuals. They are taxed two per cent of the net premiums, and the insured pays two per cent of his premium as well?

Special War Revenue Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, there is not a double
tax; there is only one.

What is meant by the
words "net premium" in this ease?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the case of mutual companies transacting business on the premium deposit plan, and reciprocal exchanges, the net premium is the net cost of insurance to the insured, together with the interest on the excess of the premium deposit, if any, over the said net cost. My hon. friend knows what that means.
I believe that is an exceedingly low rate in some cases. I understand that in some of these mutuals the net premium would be only about four per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend sees that
we are taxing about all we can tax. We are taxing the net difference as well as the interest upon the fund which remains in the hands of the company and is placed there on deposit by the insured.

I am wondering if that
is fair to the Canadian companies. You are taxing them on their net premiums, which is a far greater amount.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Paragraph as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are we taking up this resolution section by section, or are we dealing with the entire resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are taking up the insurance subsection now, and the next one will deal with the tax on telephone and telegraph messages and so on.
2. That on every cable and telegraph or radio message originating in Canada for which a charge of more than fifteen cents is made, except press despatches, and on every long distance telephone call originating in Canada for which a charge of more than fifteen cents is made the sending company shall pay to the consolidated revenue fund a tax of five cents and may charge the same to the person paying the regular charges for such message.
I wish to direct the attention of the minister to a particular case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps before my hon.
friend proceeds I should bell him that there is an amendment to be proposed, so his discussion might be more in point if the amendment is moved now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This means that in the case of charge accounts for long distance service, the monthly account will be taxed 6 per cent. In the case of pay stations, of which the Bell Telephone Company have some 19,000, whether or not there are attendants present the charge will be 5 cents for each call for which the charge is in excess of 25 cents and up to and including 80 cents,, and an additional 5 cents for each additional 80 cents.
Mr. SPEAIvMAN: Does this tax apply to provincially owned lines as well as privately owned lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Has the minister taken into consideration this instance: In New Brunswick we have farmers' telephone systems linked up with the New Brunswick Telephone Company under some special arrangement. When the farmer is connected up with the New Brunswick Telephone Company line it is charged as a long distance message. Under this measure the farmer will be compelled to pay a certain percentage of the cost of such telephone messages, while if he were using his own lines these calls would not be considered as long distance messages. If that is not looked into carefully I would say an injustice was being done the farmer who uses his own telephone system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There will be only one
tax on one telephone call.

The minister does not get
my point; it is really not a long distance call at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it is not a long distance call there will be no tax.

Let me explain it again.
It really is not a long distance call in the true sense of the word, but because of the separation of control between this company and the main line of the New Brunswick Telpnhone Company with which it connects, it
Special War Revenue Act

becomes a long distance call, because the farmer has to have permission to send his message over the line of that company. The New Brunswick Telephone Company has practically a monopoly in that province, and they need not hook up with our farm lines unless they wish to, do so. But as it is, even though the call is made over a distance of only two or three miles, it is regarded as a long distance call, and according to this legislation the farmer will be charged for a long distance message.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I must say that I do not
see the difficulty suggested by my hon. friend. The telephone companies have raised no such question.

No; they would not raise
it by any means, but if the farmers' telephone systems knew of it they would raise the point.

I want to ask a second question based upon my first, which was whether or not this tax would apply to provincially owned lines. The minister knows that a number of these telephone systems belong to and are operated by the provinces; in other words, they are crown properties in the right of the province. Has the dominion the right to tax crown property held in the right of the provinces, property controlled and operated by the government of a province and not by a private company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not taxing property held in the right of the province, we are taxing messages. The law is very clearly established that where a province engages in an undertaking of this character it shall not be exempt from taxation.
That was my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was settled in the case of Attorney General of British Columbia vs. Attorney General of Canada, reported in 1924 Appeal Cases. The liquor commission of British Columbia attempted to evade the payment of excise and customs taxes and it was found that wherever a province engages in business it is subject to taxation. I might point out to my hon. friend that the tax is being placed upon the message, and is paid by the individual and not by the company. I do not think there is any shadow of doubt on the question of the legality of the transaction.

The term "property" was used, and that is why I asked the question. I wanted to know whether or not that term included provincial governments.
vMr. Veniot.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should like to come back to the question asked by the hon. member for Gloucester and request that he give his illustration in terms of locality.

The New Brunswick Telephone Company has a central office at Caraquet, and a message to Lower Caraquet, a distance of seven miles, is not considered a long distance message. The company has a line running from Bathurst to Caraquet, and at certain points the farmers' telephones hook up with the other system. The minute the farmers' line reaches the line of the New Brunswick telephone system a message going only a mile is considered to be a long distance message.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the cost of such a message?
About fifteen or twenty-five cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say that the minimum charge would be fifteen cents under those conditions?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In that case the tax would be less than six cents on six messages.

I do not care how small the tax would be, there should be no discrimination because of a peculiar situation. This condition will be found not only in Gloucester county, but in Kent and Northumberland counties and in other sections of the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that the discrimination arises out of the tax; it apparently arises out of the attitude taken by the telephone company. Even if it were to arise out of the tax, it happens inevitably in connection with any law of general application that there are points where greater hardship will fall on one individual than on another. That is inescapable, but I may say that such a case had not hitherto been brought to my attention. If there is any way to remedy any injustice by means of regulation, that will be done.

The minister will realize that my hon. friend is referring to switching charges of five, ten or fifteen cents each, and a regulation exempting such charges up to a certain amount from the application of the tax would cover the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is a matter which
had not hitherto been brought to my attention and is entirely new to me, but I have no doubt it could be met by regulation.

Special War Revenue Act
Will the minister give his attention to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly.

According to the amendment, a copy of which the chairman has been good enough to furnish me, it would seem that a direct discrimination is being made against those who have private telephones, especially rural lines, as against those who use pay stations. A man using a pay station pays five cents if the cost of the message is over twenty-five cents; he pays nothing when the cost of the message is under that amount. A subscriber using a private rural telephone between two places where, for instance, there is a twenty cent toll, must pay six per cent on that twenty cents. I submit that such a condition is undesirable. In the first place it will mean a lot of accounting to cover a small sum and, in the second place, it is not fair that a man should be able to go to a public telephone and put through a message costing up to twenty-five cents and not have to pay, whereas a man calling on his own telephone has to pay six per cent. A message by cable, telegraph or radio originating in Canada, no matter how much it costs, pays a tax of only five cents; no ad valorem charge is made. I am not advocating that a larger tax should be imposed on cables, telegrams and radio messages; I am pointing out that the man using a private telephone-the telephone is pretty commonly used in rural communities -is penalized, while the man using a public telephone goes scot free; and the man using the cable, telegraph or radio pays only a five cent tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am advised that upwards of ninety per cent-I cannot give the exact figures-of what are known as shorter haul messages are from subscribers, and that an almost equal proportion of the messages from toll stations are what are known as longer hauls. The inequality about which my hon. friend is concerned does not seem to exist. The man sending a pay station message costing from thirty cents up to eighty cents pays five cents. If he sends three thirty cent messages he pays fifteen cents, whereas a subscriber who does ninety cents' worth of calling would pay a little less than six cents.

Take them at twenty
cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend says: take
them at twenty cents. I am told that only a fraction of the messages is of the smaller amount. If we put the toll at twenty cents, a five cent tax would be a substantial one.
That is the minimum you could charge in a toll station. Coming to the telegraph charges, I am advised that the average cost of all the telegrams sent is a little under seventy cents, so that a five cent charge, taking it on the average, is fair.

But that is not the case
with cables.
What does the minister expect to get by way of revenue from his tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Three-quarters of a million dollars from the telephone and half a million dollars from the telegraph.

I should like to ask the
minister seriously to consider a minimum below which no tax will be charged. In a public pay station, you can have a twenty-cent call and you do not pay a tax; a subscriber should be put on the same basis. My hon. friend is aware that in the province from which he and I come, there are many rural services where the tolls are from fifteen to twenty cents; I can think of a great number in my constituency. My hon. friend, possibly quite unconsciously, is penalizing those subscribers who connect up with those telephone systems. They form a little telephone company; they hitch up with the Maritime Telephone and Telegraph Company and the through rate is fifteen cents. Take for instance, from Port la Tour to Barrington, the rate is, I think, less than twenty-five cents; from Barrington Passage to Clark's Harbour, there is, I think, a ten cent toll. If a man has a telephone, there is no reason why he should have to pay a six per cent tax on those small messages, while I can go into the hotel at Barrington Passage and use the public telephone and not pay any tax to the government. The same benefit should be given to the subscriber. Just as in the case of cheques, there is a minimum of $5 below which no stamp is required, there should, in the case of telephone messages, be some minimum below which no tax is collected. I think this will be an expensive tax to collect; there, will not be a great deal of revenue from it and as drafted in the amendment it is discriminatory.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As to the revenue, I have given my hon. friend the figures. In more prosperous times the revenue would be about a million dollars.
I am speaking of the telephone message tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am told by the telephone companies that the administrative cost will be comparatively small and the method of
Special War Revenue Act

collection will not be difficult. My hon. friend spoke of the ten cent message. They could take ten of those messages before they would have to pay a six cent tax, which is not an excessive one. Admittedly this is a revenue producing measure; that is all. It has no other excuse in the world. There is no doubt it is to a large extent a nuisance tax, but it seems to me the burden in the case I have indicated is not heavy. I have in mind conditions in the province from which my hon. friend comes. Many of the local telephone companies there which cover substantial areas will not pay any tax at all. It is only when they go into the long distance telephone through the exchange of the Nova Scotia Telephone Company, that there will be any tax, and I consider, in a case of that kind, they should pay a tax.

I presume, from answers
which the minister made the hon. member for Red Deer, he is thoroughly satisfied of the right of the government to tax provincial companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not submit my own
view as being worth anything. I have consulted eminent lawyers and the Justice department have also advised me that in their judgment there is no question as to that.

In Manitoba the service is
being carried on at cost, and it is well administered. Unfortunately in these troublous times many farmers and others are taking out their telephones and I am afraid this tax will further emphasize the movement in that direction. This is something I am not worrying over, but I am afraid this tax will not help my hon. friend's friends in Manitoba in carrying out their pledge to have cheap telephones in all the farmers' houses.

The minister, I submit,
has not answered the criticism I am making. I do not want to take up the time of the committee, but it is no use for him to tell us you can put through ten messages at ten cents apiece and pay only six cents on them. A man who steps into a public telephone station can put through at least two messages and pay nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I may tell my hon. friend that those messages to which he refers constitute just four per cent of all telephone messages in Canada, so that they are a negligible quantity.

That just points the
argument I am trying to make. My hon. friend is simply imposing an irritating tax

which will not help the revenue and which is discriminatory because it is directly opposed to the principle of applying the tax to the public generally. A subscriber should not have to pay a six per cent tax on those small messages. I am again pointing out to the minister that it is useless for him to argue that it takes a lot of them to make a little money in taxes. That is just my point, and that is why I think he might just as well drop the idea and have a minimum below which he will make no charge on subscriber messages as well as on public toll station business, just as I instanced a minute ago the case of cheques, where we do not impose a stamp tax on cheques of 15 or less.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: ' My hon. friend is advocating that in the case of a percentage tax there is a minimum below which we should not go.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I originally prepared
this amendment it provided that the tax would not apply to a thirty cent message.
Fifteen cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is as it appears in
the present amendment, but I am speaking of the amendment as I devised it originally. What would the effect of that be? It would mean that three thirty cent messages would cost fifteen cents.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am referring to the
amendment as I originally proposed it. My hon. friend must get the idea into his head that there are other views than his, even if they are wrong ones. It was the telephone companies themselves who suggested this. I do not say that they are a unit throughout Canada, but I took the judgment of the great bulk of the telephone companies, and at a meeting which they held in Winnipeg representative of the telephone interests of all Canada, they were the ones who suggested to me that it would be a more equitable tax to apply the principle of the sales tax to the telephones rather than start by a five cent tax, a ten cent tax, and so on. Where you come to the dividing point between five cents and ten cents, you are going to have hardship. One man who has only one cent more to pay for a message than another, has to pay a tax of 100 per cent more. They said that it was much fairer to apply the principle of the sales tax, which would mean that you would have a percentage covering the whole

Special War Revenue Act
amount of the tax. That is why the amendment appears in its present form, and although it apparently does not convince the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, the justice of it appealed to me and that is why I am submitting it to the committee.

I have never advocated
a five cent charge. What I have been suggesting is that the ad valorem six per cent tax, if it is to be imposed, be applicable only to a message above a certain amount, and I have suggested twenty-five cents just as he has made the tax in public pay stations on twenty-five cent messages. I am not talking about a flat five cent charge and have never talked about it. My hon. friend made some remarks suggesting that I was unable to see any other views than my own.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that.

I am endeavouring to
combine my hon. friend's suggested tax of six per cent with a minimum charge just as there is in the case of stamps and cheques. If you make a six per cent charge, with a minimum, and put a rider on the resolution to the effect that no tax shall be charged on any message for which the toll is less than 25 cents, that would carry out my idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend, who is an old friend, I may say, is too shrewd not to realize that I never made the statement that he attributes to me. What I said was that my hon. friend must get the idea that there are other views than his own, even if they are wrong, which is something entirely different from what he says I said. I have got the point that my hon. friend makes as to the tax, but let me point out to him that he is pleading for a man who pays a tax of one cent. We will say that the tax should take hold at twenty cents. My hon. friend is pleading for the fifteen cent man, and he would pay a tax of less than one cent. Six fifteen-cent messages would amount to less than one dollar, so from that angle it is not worth while wasting very many words about it. I discussed the question of the cost of administration with the companies, and they told me that by simply taking the monthly accounts, without reference to amounts, other than to total them, and then charging the six per cent, it is simply a matter of bookkeeping and collection; but to go through every individual item of every account every day of the year and delete the fifteen cents on each message would involve clerical costs running into many thousands of dollars. That is why the companies made the suggestion in its present form.

There are a great many
people in the country who use. the long distance telephone very seldom, once or twice a month, perhaps less. Some have telephones and some not. Those with telephones would be able to get the call through for a cent and a fraction, but the neighbour without a telephone would have to go to the central operator and pay five cents. It is irritating for a man to pay five cents for what his neighbour gets for one cent and a fraction, and for all the difference it would make to the revenue the minister might as well drop it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know there must be good neighbours out in the hospitable west, and I would suggest in such a case as my hon. friend mentions that the man without a telephone call at his neighbour's house with a telephone and have the call charged up to his neighbour, and then he will get the call at the same cost as his neighbour.
Will the minister allow a discount of so much per mile for the distance he has to travel to his neighbour's house?

All the telephone companies would need to have would be two columns in the account, one for messages under 25 cents and the other for messages above 25 cents. Then there would be no trouble at all and no question of spending thousands of dollars as the minister suggests.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am only giving the committee the information as it was given to me by those with experience in the telephone business.
I do not think my hon. friend would say it himself.

There are four small telephone companies in the constituency I represent, and the maximum charge for calls between stations would be possibly fifteen cents. Am I to understand from the amendment that six per cent will be added to the monthly bill of tolls?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they are long distance telephone calls they would be subject to a tax of six per cent. If the account of an individual at the end of a month is $2, for instance, he will pay a tax of 12 cents.

Where a company is giving only a local service to the county, would that be called a long distance call? For instance, to get into the market town in this county costs fifteen cents, through two centrals. Would that be considered a long distance or a local call?	;
Special War Revenue Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that I can answer my hon. friend with absolute assurance. It is pretty hard to draw the line. But as I understand it, in the telephone business what is known as a long distance call is pretty well defined. If you telephone from here to Aylmer I do not understand that that is a long distance call, although I may be wrong; or if you telephone to Hintonburg that is not a long distance call. A long distance call is when you have to pay an extra toll, and I do not think it is the distance alone which governs, because, as I pointed out to my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth, there are farmers' mutuals lines in Nova Scotia, some of which extend for a great many miles, where there would be no tax at all.

In the country districts there are independent telephone companies which connect up with the Bell Telephone Company. Would such a connecting call be a long distance call and subject to the tax? That would be a great hardship in the country districts because these independent companies have some arrangement with the Bell Company whereby the farmers can telephone over a certain distance for five or ten cents. Would such a call come under this tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I find it rather difficult to give my hon. friend from Southeast Grey an answer with accuracy. The determining factor, it would seem to me, would not be whether there were two telephone companies in the transaction. If there were a connecting charge I do not think that that would have any bearing. I do not think the tax would be imposed on that charge. But if there is a charge for what is known as a long distance call, then the tax would apply. I will have careful inquiry made, but that is how it strikes me at the moment. There will be dividing lines and points where there may be some little difficulty and perhaps inequalities, but I have every hope that such cases can be met by reasonable regulations.
What does the minister understand by a long distance telephone call?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From here to Montreal, for example.
If the minister would give us a definition I think it would help relieve the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There has been no attempt at definitions so far as the department is concerned. Our idea is that we would put a tax on long distance calls as they have hitherto been known in the oustom and usage of the telephone companies.
	.

The interpretation of a long distance call may make a tremendous difference, because there are a great many districts in Ontario where the local company has to make a connection with the Bell Telephone Company to enable the farmer to reach the town in which he does business. Would the connecting charge be considered a long distance call?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think t'he connecting charge would have any bearing. It would depend on the correct interpretation of a long distance call.
Is not a long distance call a call from one exchange to another, whether they are two or five or ten or one hundred or five hundred miles apart?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope the committee does not expect me to give a technical definition, because as I have pointed out, we have attempted no definition. We propose to apply the definition recognized in the custom of telephone companies. My hon. friend should not attempt to say that a two mile call would be regarded as a long distance telephone call- not at all. Mr. Chairman, I should like to discuss in oommittee one or two matters contained in paragraph 6 of this resolution. This particular paragraph refers to the sales tax, and I notice that it has been increased from four per cent to six per oent. Two years ago the sales tax was only one per oent, and I can remember our Conservative friends in. the session of 1930 objected very strongly to the fact that the Liberal government and the Minister of Finance of that day had not done away with the sales tax altogether. They called it a poor man's tax. In spite of their arguments in 1930, the first year they were in power they increased the sales tax to four per cent. That did not satisfy them, and this year they make a further increase of fifty per cent, bringing the tax up to six per cent.
While I object very strongly to this tax in its entirety, there are one or two matters to which I take particular exception. Previous to last year an item of common consumption was on the exempted list. I refer to salt, which is used in the maritime provinces, Quebec, probably in the provinces adjoining the great lakes, and also British Columbia, for the cure of all kinds of fish. A particular brand of salt imported from foreign countries is used in this connection. As I said a minute ago, up until last year that salt was on the free list, but for some reason-and I think I am correct when I say that the then Minister of Finance merely slipped up, because I cannot understand why he would want to impose a sales tax on salt used in Canadian fisheries -the tax was put on. This salt is a raw material, and is used to cure a commodity of which 99.99 per cent is afterwards exported.
On page 25 of the Special War Revenue Act for 1931, which I now hold in my hand, the following words appear among the exemptions: "Salt, when manufactured or produced in Canada." The words, "when manufactured or produced in Canada" were added last year, and I cannot understand why the addition was made, especially in view of the fact that there is no salt produced in Canada which could be used to properly cure herring, mackerel and a great many other fish.

What about
Malagash salt?
Mr. DUFF; Malagash salt is all right for cerfcarn purposes. I am not saying a word against it, but the fact is that Malagash salt comes out of the earth, and there are certain strata in it, and when the salt is used in the curing of salt fish it leaves a scum, due to the fact that there must be earth mixed with the salt. Moreover, when the fish is cured
